prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery with a clean prediction-then-observation structure: the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model located the magic angle, and the 2018 correlated-insulator and superconducting results from the Jarillo-Herrero group showed that a twist angle tunes interaction strength. Many independent groups have reproduced the phenomenology, and the idea has spread to a whole family of moire materials. From my own work on interfaces, the central message that atomic-scale registry between two layers controls the electronic state is one I find convincing and general. Four members (Eriksson, Mehlig, Danielsson, Johansson) ranked it highly, and several of them propose the same three names, which is itself informative about where attribution lands.
statement.case_against: The microscopic origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated phases is still debated, so a citation must be worded around the flat-band platform and the observed phases and not around a mechanism. The prize might also be judged early, and the experimental credit leaves out Yuan Cao (first author of the 2018 papers) and the independent experiments of Dean, Young, Yazdani and others, which a three-name limit cannot accommodate.

responses.point: B030 (topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect) is a clean case of theory predicting a phase and experiment confirming it, with a mature and stable interpretation, and the originating theory plus first observation is the right credit.
responses.response: I agree that B030 is mature and conceptually deep, and I would not oppose it. My reservation is attribution: with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang authors all having strong claims, a three-person limit forces an exclusion that is hard to defend, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases. B021 has a tighter theory-plus-experiment split. On the point that twisted bilayer graphene may be early, I accept the interpretive uncertainty but would say the discovery of the phases is not in doubt.

responses.point: Circuit QED (B002) and trapped ions (B006) are mature, strongly confirmed routes to quantum information, though the timing relative to the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize and the Girvin allocation are open issues.
responses.response: I take the maturity point for trapped ions seriously, and B006 has a clear arc from the Cirac-Zoller proposal to Blatt's experiments. I do not rank it above B021 because Wineland and Haroche were honoured in 2012 for control of single quantum systems, and I think the committee would need a sharper argument about what is new. For B002 I agree with you that the Girvin exclusion is a genuine problem and the 2025 award makes timing awkward, so I would not choose it this year.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B024) are the clearest advance in measurement accuracy, independently confirmed at the 10^-18 level, with a clean two-person credit to Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I largely agree on the quality of B024 and ranked it third myself; attribution is cleaner there than for almost any other shortlisted candidate. Where I differ is on ordering. A clock prize rewards an invention whose payoff is in precision applications, whereas B021 opened a new field of physics. I would keep B024 as my first alternative and would support it if the committee judges that a precision-measurement prize is preferable to a materials-physics one this year.

responses.point: The Bistritzer-MacDonald model plus the 2018 experiments is a simple theoretical idea with broad experimental fallout, although the pairing mechanism is debated and Yuan Cao is outside the credited set.
responses.response: I agree, and your argument moves me on one point. I opened with only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, but the 2011 flat-band paper is a joint Bistritzer-MacDonald result, and several colleagues (you, Eriksson, Danielsson, Johansson) credit all three. I now propose all three names. On Cao, I accept that this is a real omission, but the committee cannot credit a student ahead of the group leader under the three-person rule, and I would note it in the discussion record.

responses.point: B021 is a theory-led discovery whose continuum model has been tested repeatedly, and B005 (tunnel magnetoresistance) is a close second because MgO coherent tunnelling was predicted from first principles before it was measured.
responses.response: I share your view of B021, and I take your point on B005. I know from electron microscopy how much the MgO interface structure matters, so the physics is convincing. My difficulty is the uncredited Yuasa-group contribution to giant MgO TMR and the overlap with the 2007 GMR prize, which leaves B005 as an alternative and not my preferred prize.

uncertainties: Whether the debated superconducting mechanism makes the prize premature or whether a citation about the platform and observed phases is enough.
Whether Bistritzer should share the prize with MacDonald, and how to treat Yuan Cao and other independent experimental groups under the three-person limit.
Whether the committee prefers a new-field discovery (B021) or an established measurement invention (B024) this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My connections (David R. Clarke at IBM, Chalmers colleagues, Japanese university exchanges, the microscopy federation) do not obviously involve the named candidates, though the Japan links could be checked for B005 and B024. Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which is not a conflict for any candidate.
